title: The Lighter Brief
overview: Big civic news leads today: Democrat Scott Colom won Mississippi's U.S. Senate seat in a narrow, history-making upset. Closer to home there's a proposal to split up Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools, a few Jamaica updates, a warm tribute to a civil rights pioneer, and some lighter fare, from Snoop Dogg's newest club to Voyager's first close look at Saturn's rings.

stories.headline: Scott Colom wins Mississippi's Senate seat in a historic upset
stories.summary: Democrat Scott Colom, a district attorney, narrowly beat Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, according to an Associated Press race call. He is Mississippi's first Black senator since Reconstruction and the first Democrat the state has elected to the Senate since 1982. He campaigned door to door on affordability, keeping rural hospitals open and access to healthcare. Hyde-Smith conceded, saying she respects the decision of Mississippi voters.
key_facts: Colom won by fewer than 5,000 votes, with a small share of ballots still being counted (NPR).
He is reported as the first Black U.S. senator elected by popular vote. The two earlier Black senators, both from Mississippi, were chosen by the state Legislature in the 1870s.
He also flipped traditionally Republican areas such as Forrest County.
WSOC reports Democrats now hold a 55-44 Senate edge, with Alaska's race still undecided.
stories.why: It's a milestone for Mississippi and shifts the balance of power in the U.S. Senate.

stories.headline: Rock Hill honors Willie 'Dub' Massey of the Friendship Nine
stories.summary: Willie 'Dub' Massey, one of the Friendship Nine, died Tuesday at 84. In 1961 the group held a sit-in at a segregated Rock Hill lunch counter. They chose 30 days of jail labor over paying a fine, and that 'jail, no bail' approach helped revive the student sit-in movement. A former student remembers him as a beloved sixth-grade teacher who never mentioned he was a hero.
key_facts: The 1961 fine was $100, about $1,100 in today's money.
The group served 30 days at the York County Prison Farm.
David Williamson Jr. is now the last surviving member of the Friendship Nine.
Rock Hill honored Massey with an empty seat, a plate and a glass of water.
stories.why: His quiet courage shaped history, and his community is making sure the story keeps being told.

stories.headline: Former U.S. envoy expects little change in Caribbean policy
stories.summary: Donald Tapia, a former U.S. ambassador to Jamaica, told The Gleaner he sees the midterm results as a vote against President Trump and his policies rather than against the Republican Party. Even so, he doesn't expect a reset in U.S. policy toward the Caribbean. He also discussed Kari Lake's nomination as ambassador to Jamaica and the need for U.S. immigration reform.
key_facts: Tapia is a former U.S. ambassador to Jamaica.
He urged Jamaica's political leaders to be bold in their dealings with the U.S.
stories.why: It's one informed view on how U.S. election results might, or might not, affect Jamaica.

stories.headline: Testimony continues in Jamaica's CMU fraud trial
stories.summary: A former Universal Service Fund (USF) legal officer testified that the agency's training contracts with Caribbean Maritime University (CMU) and a private institute did not provide for participants' meals. Instead, participants received a monthly stipend to cover transport and food. The trial involves former CMU President Fritz Pinnock and former Education Minister Ruel Reid, among others.
key_facts: Participants received a stipend of $10,600 a month, paid every two weeks.
The charges concern an alleged scheme to siphon more than $25 million in public funds between 2016 and 2019.
All the accused have pleaded not guilty.
The training program targeted 1,000 unemployed young people aged 18 to 35.
stories.why: The case concerns how public money for youth training was spent.

stories.headline: Holness says Jamaica may need overseas builders for rebuilding
stories.summary: Prime Minister Andrew Holness said the National Reconstruction and Resilience Authority (NaRRA) may need to bring in skilled workers from abroad to rebuild western Jamaica, because the construction industry is short of skilled labour. He spoke at a ceremony where the National Housing Trust awarded construction scholarships to 25 young Jamaicans.
key_facts: Each scholarship covers up to $1 million a year in tuition.
Holness said only about $40 billion of an $80 billion annual capital budget usually becomes physical infrastructure.
He encouraged the scholars to start their own contracting firms.
stories.why: Training young people in construction could mean more jobs and faster rebuilding.

stories.headline: Jamaican court awards woman over J$10 million for negligent dental care
stories.summary: Jamaica's Supreme Court ordered the government to pay more than J$10 million in damages to June Hyman of St Elizabeth. The case stems from a 2010 wisdom tooth extraction at a public clinic. The judge found the dentist noted Hyman's gum disease but never told her and did not order X-rays, which led to months of pain and later surgery.
key_facts: She was awarded J$7.9 million in general damages, plus interest.
Special damages include US$16,312, about J$2.5 million.
Justice Kirk Anderson described her overall treatment as 'absolutely appalling'.
stories.why: The ruling is a reminder that patients are entitled to be told about their own conditions.

stories.headline: Lawmaker plans bill to split up Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools
stories.summary: State Rep. David Willis, a Republican from Union County, plans a bill to divide Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools (CMS) into several districts. The bill would also create a way to hold recall elections for school board members. Willis says a full split would take years of study. Critics, including Rep. Laura Budd and board member Anna London, say the plan is political and would be harmful to kids. CMS is currently under state investigations into financial irregularities.
key_facts: The State Bureau of Investigation and the State Auditor's Office are both looking into CMS.
Earlier split efforts came up in 2012 and 2018.
One town mayor said his town can't afford to leave CMS.
The legislature could return as soon as next week.
stories.why: Any split would change how schooling works for many Charlotte-area families, but for now it is only a proposal.

stories.headline: Summer Walker's label countersues her as their legal fight grows
stories.summary: LVRN, Summer Walker's label and management company, has filed a countersuit saying she owes it commissions and royalties. This follows her August lawsuit accusing LVRN of mishandling her money. She is also in a separate legal fight with Interscope over leaving her record deal.
key_facts: LVRN says it is owed a 7% cut of her tour, 20% of her performance royalties and a 15% management commission.
Interscope sued in October for at least $50 million.
A hearing in the Interscope case is set for April 15.
disputed: Every claim on both sides is an allegation, and nothing has been proven in court.
LVRN denies Walker's claims that it diverted her money.
Walker disputes Interscope's claim that she still owes albums.
stories.why: It shows how complicated it can be for an artist to leave a long-term music deal.
